title: Why Campo de Calatrava tastes the way it does

lede.text: Campo de Calatrava is the most important place in Iberia where volcanoes have erupted in recent times. Its dark soils bring the vines on early, which lets the fruit ripen over a longer cycle.

chapters.title: Volcanoes among quartzite ridges
paras: The land lies at the south-eastern end of the Iberian Massif. Its volcanic rock sits in the centre of Ciudad Real province. Wide basins sit between ridges of quartzite. More than 240 volcanoes dot the land, on the basin floors as well as on the ridge tops and foothills.
The eruptions came in two main phases, 8.5 to 6.5 million years ago and 4.5 to 1.5 million years ago. The volcanic rock spreads over about 4,500 to 5,000 km2. Vineyards cover 13,583.71 ha of it.
Some blasts, where magma met water, left maars. These are wide and deep craters ringed by tuff or by high walls of quartzite. When the weather allows, many of them hold water and make wetlands.
The country is rolling. Gentle long rises at 700 to 900 m alternate with small plains at about 630 to 650 m.

chapters.title: Dry air under a bright sky
paras: The year averages 15.6 °C, with highs of 21.7 °C and lows of 9.5 °C. Sunshine tops 2,800 hours a year.
The Montes de Toledo and the Sierra Morena stand on either side. Their Föhn effect largely keeps clouds away and rain low.

Rain barely reaches 400 mm a year and relative humidity averages 52%. The risk of damp-related vine disease is practically nil. Days with more than 10 mm of rain average no more than two a month. That keeps off fungi such as downy mildew, and powdery mildew is less likely.
Summer water is scarce. The maars may help here. Their water and wetlands could soften some of the harshest conditions of the climate.

chapters.title: Dark, stony soil with its own fingerprint
paras: The soils fall into 6 FAO groups, a variety that marks the area out. Their dark colour takes in more of the sun's radiation. That favours a warmer soil, which makes it early ground for the vine.
Some profiles are very stony at the surface. The subsoil is mostly clay loam, which lets roots grow well and stores water.

In the topsoil, calcium is low, at 88.9 g/kg against 301.0 g/kg for Castilla-La Mancha and the world. Potassium is high, at 20.3 g/kg against 15.4 g/kg. Manganese sits above normal levels for Castilla-La Mancha. Iron and zinc are above the regional average too.

Nickel is nearly double the world average and more than triple that of Castilla-La Mancha. It comes from the ground's own chemistry, not from human pollution. Six other elements, vanadium and chromium among them, are also well above regional and world averages.

Together they form a geochemical fingerprint that comes from the area's volcanic past. The wines take distinctive mineral components from it. Soil and climate together make mineral notes possible in the glass.

chapters.title: Many grapes, five kinds of wine
paras: Growers plant a wide mix of grapes. Ten red grapes are allowed, Cencibel (Tempranillo) among them. Eleven white grapes are allowed, Airén among them. Low calcium lets growers choose among more rootstocks.

Water is tightly limited, so many vineyards are dry-farmed. The classic training is en vaso, a free-standing bush that copes better without irrigation. It is typical of Airén and Cencibel vineyards. Yields are capped at 10,000 kg/ha for bush vines and 13,000 kg/ha for trellised ones. Vine and olive together are a typical pairing here.

Still wines come in white, rosado (rosé) and red. Each can be dry, semi-dry, semi-sweet or sweet, from 4 g/l of sugar or less to over 45 g/l. Reds can be young or aged. The three aged grades are Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva. Crianza needs 24 months of ageing, with at least 6 in oak barrels of up to 330 litres. Reserva needs 36 months, with at least 12 in barrel. Gran Reserva needs 60 months, with at least 18 in barrel.

Roble reds spend at least 60 days in oak. They smell of red and black fruit with spice. At least one more aroma family joins in, such as toast or nuts. Clásico whites and reds ferment in concrete or ceramic tanks, or in tinajas, the big clay jars. They are bright wines with floral or fruity aromas.

Sparkling white and rosé come from the traditional method or the Charmat method. Seven sweetness terms are allowed. The driest is Brut nature, under 3 g/l, with no sugar added after the second fermentation. Brut is under 12 g/l. Seco, which means dry, is 17 to 32 g/l. The sweetest is Dulce, over 50 g/l.

The last kind is an over-ripe red. The grapes over-ripen on the vine until they hold enough sugar for at least 16% vol. The wine keeps at least 5 g/l of sugar. It then ages at least 8 years in oak barrels of 225 to 500 litres. Warm, bright autumns favour this over-ripening. Strong sun at ripening time helps, with dry air and little rain. The wine smells at least of stewed fruit and toast, with spice.

The wines are balanced, structured and fresh. They are high in alcohol and deep in colour. Early soils and the water conditions let the grapes ripen longer, which concentrates what gives that alcohol and colour. The long ripening favours their aromatic complexity. Very high sunshine and the potassium in the soil add to it.
